claim: OSCA/TMEM63s are a newly-identified family of eukaryotic mechanically activated ion channels opened by membrane tension.
source: OSCA/TMEM63s are a newly-identified family of eukaryotic mechanically activated ion channels opened by membrane tension.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a companion paper (Murthy et al., 2018) that characterizes these proteins as mechanically activated ion channels.

claim: OSCA1.2 has a dimeric architecture.
source: The structure of OSCA1.2 reveals a trapezoid-shaped homodimer with a two-fold symmetry axis perpendicular to the membrane (Figure 1A–H).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 1.

claim: OSCA1.2 contains eleven transmembrane helices per subunit.
source: Here, we elucidate high resolution cryo-electron microscopy structures of OSCA1.2, revealing a dimeric architecture containing eleven transmembrane helices per subunit and surprising topological similarities to TMEM16 proteins.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure determination and model building described in the manuscript.

claim: OSCA1.2 has topological similarities to TMEM16 proteins.
source: Here, we elucidate high resolution cryo-electron microscopy structures of OSCA1.2, revealing a dimeric architecture containing eleven transmembrane helices per subunit and surprising topological similarities to TMEM16 proteins.
evidence: The structural comparison between OSCA1.2 and TMEM16 proteins is demonstrated through cryo-EM data and structural alignment.

claim: A conserved acidic residue (E531) is a determinant of OSCA1.2 channel conductance.
source: We locate the ion permeation pathway within each subunit by demonstrating that a conserved acidic residue is a determinant of channel conductance.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experiments showing that E531A mutation decreases single-channel conductance by 1.6-fold.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations reveal membrane interactions suggesting the role of lipids in OSCA1.2 gating.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations reveal membrane interactions, suggesting the role of lipids in OSCA1.2 gating.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data showing lipid molecules occupying specific regions of the protein structure.

claim: Plants with mutant OSCA1 have impaired osmotic stress signaling.
source: Plants with mutant OSCA1 have impaired osmotic stress signaling (Yuan et al., 2014), implying that OSCAs function as sensors of osmotic-stress induced mechanical force in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yuan et al., 2014.

claim: TMEM63 proteins are animal orthologues of OSCA that produce MA currents when expressed in naïve cells.
source: TMEM63 proteins are animal orthologues of OSCA that produce MA currents when expressed in naïve cells (Murthy et al., 2018), but their physiological roles remain undetermined.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the companion paper Murthy et al., 2018.

claim: Cryo-EM reconstructions of OSCA1.2 in lipidic nanodiscs were determined at 3.1 Å resolution.
source: We purified Arabidopsis thaliana OSCA1.2 expressed in HEK293F cells and determined cryo-EM reconstructions in lipidic nanodiscs and Lauryl Maltose Neopentyl Glycol (LMNG) detergent micelle with cholesteryl hemisuccinate (CHS) at 3.1 and 3.5 Å resolution, respectively (Figure 1A–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by the cryo-EM data collection and processing described in the methods.

claim: Cryo-EM reconstructions of OSCA1.2 in LMNG detergent micelle with CHS were determined at 3.5 Å resolution.
source: We purified Arabidopsis thaliana OSCA1.2 expressed in HEK293F cells and determined cryo-EM reconstructions in lipidic nanodiscs and Lauryl Maltose Neopentyl Glycol (LMNG) detergent micelle with cholesteryl hemisuccinate (CHS) at 3.1 and 3.5 Å resolution, respectively (Figure 1A–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by the cryo-EM data collection and processing described in the methods.

claim: The resulting density maps allowed building of 82% of the full-length OSCA1.2 sequence.
source: The resulting density maps allowed building of 82% of the full-length OSCA1.2 sequence (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the model building process and the quality of the cryo-EM maps.

claim: Structures of OSCA1.2 in nanodisc and LMNG were nearly identical (RMSD = 0.81 Å).
source: Structures of OSCA1.2 in nanodisc and LMNG were nearly identical (RMSD = 0.81 Å, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: The purified OSCA1.2 channel reconstituted in liposomes retains MA ion channel activity.
source: Importantly, the purified channel reconstituted in liposomes retains MA ion channel activity (Murthy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by functional assays described in the companion paper.

claim: The OSCA1.2 dimer is 139 Å across at its widest dimension.
source: The dimer is 139 Å across at its widest dimension.
evidence: This measurement is derived from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The transmembrane domain of each OSCA1.2 monomer contains eleven TM helices.
source: The bulk of the protein lies within the membrane; the transmembrane (TM) domain (TMD) of each monomer contains eleven TM helices.
evidence: This is determined from the cryo-EM structure and model building.

claim: The intracellular domain of OSCA1.2 extends ~31 Å below the membrane.
source: Linkers between TM helices and a C-terminal region come together to form an intracellular domain (ICD) that extends ~31 Å below the membrane (Figure 1A–H).
evidence: This measurement is derived from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The ICD contributes the sole dimeric interface in OSCA1.2, with a buried surface area of 1,331 Å2.
source: The ICD contributes the sole dimeric interface in OSCA1.2, with a buried surface area of 1,331 Å2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D) (Krissinel and Henrick, 2007), only 4% of the total surface area of the dimer.
evidence: This is calculated from the structure using established methods.

claim: Within the membrane, inter-subunit contacts in OSCA1.2 are nonexistent.
source: Within the membrane, inter-subunit contacts are nonexistent.
evidence: This is observed from the cryo-EM structure showing a cleft between subunits.

claim: A cleft with minimum width of approximately 8 Å separates one OSCA1.2 subunit's TMD from the other.
source: Instead, a cleft with minimum width of approximately 8 Å separates one subunit's TMD from the other (Figure 1I).
evidence: This measurement is derived from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: AT-MD simulations of OSCA1.2 in a POPC bilayer consistently place lipid molecules inside the inter-subunit cleft.
source: Interestingly, AT-MD simulations of OSCA1.2 in a phospholipid (1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine, POPC) bilayer, consistently place lipid molecules inside the cleft (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 5A, Video 2), indicating a role for lipids in stabilizing the dimeric assembly.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Lipids play a role in stabilizing the dimeric assembly of OSCA1.2.
source: Interestingly, AT-MD simulations of OSCA1.2 in a phospholipid (1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine, POPC) bilayer, consistently place lipid molecules inside the cleft (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 5A, Video 2), indicating a role for lipids in stabilizing the dimeric assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from MD simulation results showing lipids occupying the inter-subunit cleft.

claim: The N-terminus of OSCA1.2 faces the extracellular environment.
source: The N-terminus of OSCA1.2 faces the extracellular environment while the C-terminus is intracellular.
evidence: This topology is determined from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The C-terminus of OSCA1.2 is intracellular.
source: The N-terminus of OSCA1.2 faces the extracellular environment while the C-terminus is intracellular.
evidence: This topology is determined from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The majority of the ICD is comprised of the second intracellular linker (IL2), which is over 150 residues.
source: The majority of the ICD is comprised of the second intracellular linker (IL2), which is over 150 residues and contains a 4-stranded antiparallel ß-sheet (IL2ß1-IL2ß4) with well-conserved sequences across the OSCA family (Figure 2—figure supplements 1, 2 and 3), and four helices (IL2H1-IL2H4).
evidence: This is determined from the cryo-EM structure and sequence analysis.

claim: IL2 contains a 4-stranded antiparallel ß-sheet (IL2ß1-IL2ß4) with well-conserved sequences across the OSCA family.
source: The majority of the ICD is comprised of the second intracellular linker (IL2), which is over 150 residues and contains a 4-stranded antiparallel ß-sheet (IL2ß1-IL2ß4) with well-conserved sequences across the OSCA family (Figure 2—figure supplements 1, 2 and 3), and four helices (IL2H1-IL2H4).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Ten of the eleven TM helices of OSCA1.2 closely follow the topology and organization of mouse TMEM16A Ca2+-activated chloride channel.
source: Strikingly, our structure reveals that the structural homology extends beyond the C-terminal region; ten of the eleven TM helices of OSCA1.2 closely follow the topology and organization of mouse TMEM16A (mTMEM16A) Ca2+-activated chloride channel (Dang et al., 2017; Paulino et al., 2017a; Paulino et al., 2017b) and Nectria haematococca TMEM16 (nhTMEM16), which is a Ca2+-dependent lipid scramblase (Brunner et al., 2014) and nonselective ion channel (Lee et al., 2016) (Figure 2C; Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A; Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison with published TMEM16 structures.

claim: OSCA1.2 has an additional N-terminal TM helix (TM0) positioned at the periphery of the TMD relative to TMEM16 structures.
source: Relative to these TMEM16 structures, OSCA1.2 has an additional N-terminal TM helix positioned at the periphery of the TMD (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed from structural comparison between OSCA1.2 and TMEM16 proteins.

claim: The relative orientation of one OSCA1.2 subunit to the other is different from TMEM16A.
source: Though TM1-TM10 of OSCA1.2 and TMEM16A align well at the level of a single subunit, the relative orientation of one subunit to the other is different (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural alignment and comparison.

claim: The TMD of the OSCA1.2 dimer is more than 20 Å wider than mTMEM16A or nhTMEM16.
source: As a result of this distinct dimeric packing, the TMD of the OSCA1.2 dimer is more than 20 Å wider than mTMEM16A or nhTMEM16.
evidence: This measurement is derived from structural comparison.

claim: The intracellular domain of OSCA1.2 is mostly comprised of IL2, which connects TM2 and TM3.
source: First, the intracellular domain of OSCA1.2 is mostly comprised of IL2, which connects TM2 and TM3, while the intracellular domains of mTMEM16a and nhTMEM16 are formed primarily by the N- and C- termini.
evidence: This is observed from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The regulatory Ca2+ binding site conserved across the TMEM16 family does not have a chemical environment conducive for Ca2+ binding in OSCA1.2.
source: Second, the regulatory Ca2+ binding site composed of acidic and polar residues conserved across the TMEM16 family (Brunner et al., 2014) does not have a chemical environment conducive for Ca2+ binding in OSCA1.2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C), consistent with distinct modes of regulation (mechanical activation vs. Ca2+ dependence).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and comparison with TMEM16 Ca2+ binding sites.

claim: OSCA1.2 has two pores, one within each subunit.
source: Topological similarities with mTMEM16A (Figure 2) suggest that OSCA1.2 also has two pores and could conduct ions through a structurally analogous pathway lined by TM3-TM7.
evidence: This is inferred from structural similarity to TMEM16A and supported by mutagenesis data.

claim: The existence of two pores per OSCA1.2 dimer is consistent with the presence of a single subconductance state in stretch-activated single-channel currents.
source: The existence of two pores per OSCA1.2 dimer is consistent with the presence of a single subconductance state in stretch-activated single-channel currents (Murthy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data from the companion paper.

claim: The putative pore of OSCA1.2 has an opening greater than 12 Å wide towards the extracellular side.
source: Towards the extracellular side, this putative pore has an opening greater than 12 Å wide, which narrows into a 'neck' approximately 15 Å down the conduction pathway (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is calculated using the HOLE program on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The neck of the OSCA1.2 pore extends for over 10 Å and reaches a minimum van der Waals radius of 0.5 Å, closing the channel.
source: The neck extends for over 10 Å and reaches a minimum van der Waals radius of 0.5 Å, closing the channel.
evidence: This is calculated using the HOLE program on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Mostly hydrophobic residues (I393, V396, A400, L434, L438, F471, V476, and F515) line the pore's constriction.
source: Mostly hydrophobic residues (I393, V396, A400, L434, L438, F471, V476, and F515) line the pore's constriction, as well as several charged and polar residues (Q397, S480, Y468, K512, and D523).
evidence: This is determined from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: A pair of π-helical turns (in TM5 and TM6a) are nearby the pore's neck region.
source: Interestingly, a pair of π-helical turns (in TM5 and TM6a) are nearby the pore's neck region (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is observed from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: π-to-α transitions at the π-helical turn positions could be associated with gating and, potentially, channel opening.
source: Because π-helices are energetically unstable, we speculate that π-to-α transitions at these positions could be associated with gating and, potentially, channel opening.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known instability of π-helices and structural observations.

claim: There are π-helical turns at highly similar locations of TM6 in mTMEM16A and nhTMEM16.
source: In support of this idea, there are π-helical turns at highly similar locations of TM6 in mTMEM16A (Paulino et al., 2017a) and nhTMEM16 (Brunner et al., 2014), and a α-to-π transition in TM6 underlies Ca2+-dependent activation in mTMEM16A (Paulino et al., 2017a) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is supported by published structures of TMEM16 proteins.

claim: A α-to-π transition in TM6 underlies Ca2+-dependent activation in mTMEM16A.
source: In support of this idea, there are π-helical turns at highly similar locations of TM6 in mTMEM16A (Paulino et al., 2017a) and nhTMEM16 (Brunner et al., 2014), and a α-to-π transition in TM6 underlies Ca2+-dependent activation in mTMEM16A (Paulino et al., 2017a) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is supported by published structural studies of TMEM16A.

claim: The pore-lining helices of the epithelial calcium channel TRPV6 undergo π-to-α helix transitions during gating.
source: Similarly, the pore-lining helices of the epithelial calcium channel TRPV6 (McGoldrick et al., 2018) undergo π-to-α helix transitions during gating.
evidence: This is supported by citation to McGoldrick et al., 2018.

claim: Below the neck, the OSCA1.2 pore widens, and the side chains of E531, R572, and T568 create a hydrophilic environment that could stabilize hydrated ions.
source: Directly below the neck, the pore widens, and the side chains of E531, R572, and T568 create a hydrophilic environment that could stabilize hydrated ions (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is observed from the cryo-EM structure and represents a hypothesis about ion stabilization.

claim: E531A mutation decreased the stretch-activated single-channel conductance by 1.6-fold.
source: Strikingly, the mutation decreased the stretch-activated single-channel conductance by 1.6-fold, demonstrating that E531 contributes to the channel's ion permeation pathway (Figure 3F,G), and could play a role in binding or sequestering cations.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological measurements comparing wildtype and mutant channels.

claim: E531 contributes to the channel's ion permeation pathway.
source: Strikingly, the mutation decreased the stretch-activated single-channel conductance by 1.6-fold, demonstrating that E531 contributes to the channel's ion permeation pathway (Figure 3F,G), and could play a role in binding or sequestering cations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the functional effect of the E531A mutation on conductance.

claim: E531 could play a role in binding or sequestering cations.
source: Strikingly, the mutation decreased the stretch-activated single-channel conductance by 1.6-fold, demonstrating that E531 contributes to the channel's ion permeation pathway (Figure 3F,G), and could play a role in binding or sequestering cations.
evidence: This is inferred from the acidic nature of E531 and its effect on conductance.

claim: TM3-TM7 most likely form the pore of OSCA1.2.
source: Nonetheless, combining these mutagenesis data with structural homology to mTMEM16A (Paulino et al., 2017a; Paulino et al., 2017b), we conclude that TM3-TM7 most likely form the pore.
evidence: This conclusion is based on mutagenesis data, structural homology to TMEM16A, and MD simulations.

claim: MD simulations show hydration of the pore pathway being consistent with the pore radius profile from HOLE.
source: This conclusion is further supported by MD simulations showing hydration of the pore pathway being consistent with the pore radius profile from HOLE (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Video 4, Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: OSCA1.2 has a hook-shaped loop that enters the membrane that intervenes IL2H2 and IL2H3.
source: Two notable features present in OSCA1.2, but not TMEM16s, are a hook-shaped loop that enters the membrane that intervenes IL2H2 and IL2H3 (Figure 2A, Figure 4A), and a horizontal amphipathic helix in IL1 (IL1H1) that slightly deforms the membrane lower leaflet in MD simulations (Figure 4B, Video 1).
evidence: This is observed from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: OSCA1.2 has a horizontal amphipathic helix in IL1 (IL1H1) that slightly deforms the membrane lower leaflet in MD simulations.
source: Two notable features present in OSCA1.2, but not TMEM16s, are a hook-shaped loop that enters the membrane that intervenes IL2H2 and IL2H3 (Figure 2A, Figure 4A), and a horizontal amphipathic helix in IL1 (IL1H1) that slightly deforms the membrane lower leaflet in MD simulations (Figure 4B, Video 1).
evidence: This is observed from MD simulation data.

claim: The hook and IL1H1 could be sensitive to membrane tension.
source: Their association with the cytoplasmic bilayer leaflet suggests these two features could be sensitive to membrane tension, akin to the N-terminal amphipathic helix in MscL (Bavi et al., 2016), and their movement could be coupled to channel conformation through their interactions with the TMD (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is inferred from their structural features and comparison to MscL.

claim: The lower region of the OSCA1.2 pore is exposed to the membrane and could permit lipid entry.
source: Another notable aspect of the OSCA1.2 structure, similar to TMEM16s, is that the lower region of the pore is exposed to the membrane and thus could permit lipid entry (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is observed from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: In MD simulations, lipids occupy and occlude the cytoplasmic half of the OSCA1.2 pore.
source: Indeed, in MD simulations, lipids occupy and occlude the cytoplasmic half of the pore, with their phosphate head groups interacting with four lysine residues on TM4 and TM6b (Figure 4C, Figure 1—figure supplement 5C, Video 6, Video 7).
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Membrane tension might promote gating by affecting the lipid occupancy in the cytoplasmic pore region.
source: It is possible that membrane tension promotes gating by affecting the lipid occupancy in this region, analogous to proposed mechanistic models for TRAAK (Brohawn et al., 2014) and MscS (Pliotas et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on observations from MD simulations and comparison to other mechanosensitive channels.

claim: A general principle of MA ion channels is that their cross-sectional area should increase in response to membrane tension.
source: Finally, a general principle of MA ion channels is that their cross-sectional area should increase in response to membrane tension (Guo and MacKinnon, 2017; Haswell et al., 2011; Phillips et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the field of mechanosensitive channels.

claim: The absence of a dimeric protein-protein interface between membrane domains could allow OSCA1.2 to expand its cross-sectional area significantly in response to physiological lateral tension.
source: Qualitatively, the absence of a dimeric protein-protein interface between membrane domains (Figure 1I) could allow OSCA1.2 to expand its cross-sectional area significantly in response to physiological lateral tension without the energetic penalty of breaking inter-subunit interactions within the membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation of the inter-subunit cleft.

claim: Transmembrane-channel-like (TMC) proteins are pore-forming subunits of the hair cell mechanoelectrical transduction (MET) apparatus.
source: Intriguingly, transmembrane-channel-like (TMC) proteins, which are pore-forming subunits of the hair cell mechanoelectrical transduction (MET) apparatus (Fettiplace, 2016; Kawashima et al., 2011; Pan et al., 2013), are distantly related to the TMEM16 family and proposed to have the same topology (Ballesteros et al., 2018; Hahn et al., 2009; Medrano-Soto et al., 2018; Pan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TMC proteins are distantly related to the TMEM16 family and proposed to have the same topology.
source: Intriguingly, transmembrane-channel-like (TMC) proteins, which are pore-forming subunits of the hair cell mechanoelectrical transduction (MET) apparatus (Fettiplace, 2016; Kawashima et al., 2011; Pan et al., 2013), are distantly related to the TMEM16 family and proposed to have the same topology (Ballesteros et al., 2018; Hahn et al., 2009; Medrano-Soto et al., 2018; Pan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The shared TM topology between TMEM16s and OSCA1.2 suggests a similar fold for TMCs.
source: Although the molecular identity of the MET ion channel remains incompletely understood (Fettiplace, 2016), the shared TM topology between more distantly related TMEM16s and OSCA1.2 suggests a similar fold for TMCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural similarities observed between OSCA1.2 and TMEM16 proteins.

claim: OSCA/TMEM63, TMEM16, and TMC all likely utilize a similar architectural scaffold to carry out various functions at the membrane.
source: It is therefore likely that OSCA/TMEM63, TMEM16, and TMC all utilize a similar architectural scaffold to carry out various functions at the membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural similarities and evolutionary relationships.

claim: E531A had maximal current responses comparable to wildtype OSCA1.2 channels.
source: E531A had maximal current responses comparable to wildtype channels (Figure 3D,E), and modestly faster inactivation kinetics (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: E531A had modestly faster inactivation kinetics compared to wildtype OSCA1.2.
source: E531A had maximal current responses comparable to wildtype channels (Figure 3D,E), and modestly faster inactivation kinetics (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological measurements showing inactivation time constants.

claim: E531 is the only pore-facing acidic residue conserved in the pore region across the OSCA/TMEM63 families.
source: We chose to examine E531, which is the only pore-facing acidic residue conserved in this region across the OSCA/TMEM63 families and thus could contribute to conductance (Figure 3C, Figure 2—figure supplements 1, 2 and 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis across the OSCA/TMEM63 family.

claim: Cryo-EM structures of two other members of the OSCA/TMEM63 family, OSCA1.1 and OSCA3.1, were recently published after the initial BioRxiv deposition.
source: We note that cryo-EM structures of two other members of the OSCA/TMEM63 family, OSCA1.1 and OSCA3.1 (Zhang et al., 2018), were recently published after our initial BioRxiv deposition (Jojoa-Cruz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the publication timeline and is supported by citations.

claim: The model includes residues 3–50, 71–122, 156–401, 420–490, 502–717, totaling 634 of 771 residues in the full-length sequence of OSCA1.2.
source: In each structure, the model includes residues 3–50, 71–122, 156–401, 420–490, 502–717, totaling 634 of 771 residues in the full-length sequence of OSCA1.2.
evidence: This is stated in the model building section of the methods.

claim: Codon optimized OSCA1.2 gene for expression in human cell lines was cloned into vector pcDNA3.1.
source: For structural studies, codon optimized OSCA1.2 gene (UniProt ID: Q5XEZ5) for expression in human cell lines was cloned into vector pcDNA3.1.
evidence: This is described in the methods section.

claim: An EGFP tag was placed at the C terminus of OSCA1.2 and connected via a PreScission Protease cleavable linker.
source: An EGFP tag was placed at the C terminus and connected to the gene via a PreScission Protease cleavable linker (LEVLFQGP).
evidence: This is described in the methods section.

claim: Typical yields of OSCA1.2 using the LMNG purification procedure were ~60 µg purified product per liter of HEK293F cells.
source: Typical yields of OSCA1.2 using this procedure were ~60 µg purified product per liter of HEK293F cells.
evidence: This is stated in the protein purification methods.

claim: Typical yields of OSCA1.2 in nanodiscs using the nanodisc purification procedure were ~30 µg purified product per liter of HEK293F cells.
source: Typical yields of OSCA1.2 in nanodiscs using this procedure were ~30 µg purified product per liter of HEK293F cells.
evidence: This is stated in the protein purification methods.

claim: The E531 mutation could alter pore structure and dynamics owing to the interactions of the E531 side chain with R572 and Y605.
source: Alternatively, the mutation could alter pore structure and dynamics owing to the interactions of the E531 side chain with R572 and Y605 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations of E531 interactions.

claim: The PP-EGFP fusion at the C-terminus of OSCA1.2 did not affect channel expression or MA current properties.
source: The PP-EGFP fusion at the C-terminus of the protein did not affect channel expression or MA current properties.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the construct used for electrophysiology.

claim: Cryo-EM maps of OSCA1.2 in nanodiscs have been deposited to the Electron Microscopy Data Bank under accession code 9112.
source: Cryo-EM maps of OSCA1.2 in nanodiscs and LMNG have been deposited to the Electron Microscopy Data Bank under accession codes 9112 and 9113.
evidence: This is stated in the data availability section.

claim: Cryo-EM maps of OSCA1.2 in LMNG have been deposited to the Electron Microscopy Data Bank under accession code 9113.
source: Cryo-EM maps of OSCA1.2 in nanodiscs and LMNG have been deposited to the Electron Microscopy Data Bank under accession codes 9112 and 9113.
evidence: This is stated in the data availability section.

claim: Atomic coordinates of OSCA1.2 in nanodiscs have been deposited to the PDB under ID 6MGV.
source: Atomic coordinates of OSCA1.2 in nanodiscs and LMNG have been deposited to the PDB under IDs 6MGV and 6MGW.
evidence: This is stated in the data availability section.

claim: Atomic coordinates of OSCA1.2 in LMNG have been deposited to the PDB under ID 6MGW.
source: Atomic coordinates of OSCA1.2 in nanodiscs and LMNG have been deposited to the PDB under IDs 6MGV and 6MGW.
evidence: This is stated in the data availability section.

claim: Mechanically activated ion channels underlie touch, hearing, shear-stress sensing, and response to turgor pressure.
source: Mechanically activated ion channels underlie touch, hearing, shear-stress sensing, and response to turgor pressure.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of mechanosensation.

claim: Mechanical stimuli such as touch, gravity, and osmotic pressure are sensed by mechanically activated (MA) ion channels.
source: Mechanical stimuli such as touch, gravity, and osmotic pressure are sensed by mechanically activated (MA) ion channels (Haswell et al., 2011; Ranade et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: OSCA/TMEM63 are not homologous to other known MA ion channels.
source: OSCA/TMEM63 are not homologous to other known MA ion channels, and no previous study has addressed their molecular structure.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents the novelty of the study.

claim: No previous study has addressed the molecular structure of OSCA/TMEM63 proteins.
source: OSCA/TMEM63 are not homologous to other known MA ion channels, and no previous study has addressed their molecular structure.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents the novelty of the study.

claim: In MD simulations, intermittent permeation of water between L434 (TM4) and Y519 (TM6) was observed in subunit 1 when position restraints were removed after 50 ns.
source: In subunit 1, intermittent permeation of water between L434 (TM4) and Y519 (TM6) were observed when position restraints were removed after 50 ns.
evidence: This is observed from molecular dynamics simulation data described in Video 4 caption.

claim: Subunit 2 of OSCA1.2 remains impermeable to water during the entire MD simulation.
source: Subunit 2 remains impermeable to water during the entire simulation, in contrast to that in subunit 1 (Video 4).
evidence: This is observed from molecular dynamics simulation data described in Video 5 caption.

claim: The orientation of K435 rearranges to face the constricted region of the pore after the position restraints are removed after 50 ns in both subunits.
source: For both of the subunits, the orientation of K435 rearranges to face the constricted region of the pore after the position restraints are removed after 50 ns.
evidence: This is observed from molecular dynamics simulation data described in Video 6 caption.

claim: Lipid flip-flop (scramblase activity) was not observed over the course of the MD simulation.
source: Lipid flip-flop (i.e. scramblase activity) was not observed over the course of the simulation.
evidence: This is observed from molecular dynamics simulation data described in Video 1 caption.

claim: The outer leaflet of the bilayer in the inter-subunit cleft region contains 18 PC molecules whilst the inner leaflet contains 14 molecules.
source: (A) Side view of the PC molecules in contact with both subunits at the dimer interface cleft, revealing an asymmetric bilayer between subunits. The outer leaflet of the bilayer in this region contains 18 PC molecules whilst the inner leaflet contains 14 molecules.
evidence: This is determined from molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: The upper and lower leaflets in the inter-subunit cleft contain 13 and 9 POPC molecules respectively at the start of the AT simulation.
source: Here the upper and lower leaflets contain 13 and 9 POPC molecules respectively.
evidence: This is determined from molecular dynamics simulation data described in Video 2 caption.

claim: The networks of lipids in both leaflets of the inter-subunit cleft are stable during the simulation.
source: The networks of lipids in both leaflets are stable. No lipids either entered or left the cleft.
evidence: This is observed from molecular dynamics simulation data described in Video 2 caption.

claim: Phosphate head groups of lipids are within hydrogen-bonding distance of lysine residues K435, K450, K536, and K544.
source: (C) Left, a snapshot (also see Figure 4C) highlighting five lipids residing at the cytoplasmic side of the pore taken at 250 ns of the AT-MD simulation. Right, the same snapshot with the lipid phosphates highlighted and the lysine amine nitrogen to phosphate oxygen distance measured in Å, suggesting phosphate head groups are within hydrogen-bonding distance of the lysine residues.
evidence: This is determined from molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5C.
